title: Chapter 10 — Of The Taste For Physical Well-Being In America
paragraphs: In America the passion for physical well-being is not always exclusive, but it is general; and if all do not feel it in the same way, it is felt by all. To satisfy carefully all, even the smallest wants of the body, and to provide the little conveniences of life, is uppermost in every mind. Something of the same character is more and more apparent in Europe. Among the causes that produce these similar consequences in both hemispheres, several are so closely connected with my subject that they deserve notice.

When wealth is fixed in families by inheritance, there are a great number of men who enjoy the comforts of life without feeling an exclusive taste for them. The human heart is not so much caught by the undisturbed possession of anything valuable as by the desire—still imperfectly satisfied—of possessing it, and by the constant fear of losing it. In aristocratic communities, the wealthy, never having known any condition different from their own, have no fear of changing it. The existence of such conditions hardly occurs to them. The comforts of life are not for them the end of life, but simply a way of living; they regard them as existence itself—enjoyed, but scarcely thought about. Since the natural and instinctive taste all men feel for being well off is thus satisfied without trouble and without anxiety, their faculties are turned elsewhere, and fasten onto more arduous and lofty undertakings that excite and engross their minds. That is why, in the midst of physical gratifications, the members of an aristocracy often display a haughty contempt for these very enjoyments, and show singular powers of endurance when deprived of them. All the revolutions that have ever shaken or destroyed aristocracies have shown how easily men accustomed to superfluous luxuries can do without the necessities of life; whereas men who have toiled to acquire a competence can hardly live once they have lost it.

If I shift my observation from the upper to the lower classes, I find similar effects produced by opposite causes. In a nation where aristocracy predominates in society and keeps it stationary, the people in the end grow as accustomed to poverty as the rich to their opulence. The rich spend no anxiety on their physical comforts because they enjoy them without effort; the poor do not think of things they despair of obtaining, and which they hardly know well enough even to desire. In communities of this kind, the imagination of the poor is driven to seek another world. The miseries of real life surround it, but it escapes their control and flies off to seek its pleasures far beyond. When, on the contrary, the distinctions of rank are blurred and privileges destroyed—when hereditary property is subdivided, and education and freedom are widely diffused—the desire to acquire the comforts of the world haunts the imagination of the poor, and the fear of losing them haunts that of the rich. Many small fortunes spring up; those who possess them have a sufficient share of physical gratifications to develop a taste for these pleasures, but not enough to satisfy it. They never get them without effort, and they never indulge in them without anxiety. They are therefore always straining to pursue or to retain gratifications so delightful, so imperfect, so fleeting.

If I were to ask what passion is most natural to men who are both stimulated and restricted by the obscurity of their birth or the mediocrity of their fortune, I could find none more peculiarly suited to their condition than this love of physical prosperity. The passion for physical comforts is essentially a passion of the middle classes: with those classes it grows and spreads, with them it predominates. From them it rises into the higher orders of society and descends into the mass of the people. I never met a citizen in America so poor that he did not cast a glance of hope and envy on the enjoyments of the rich, nor whose imagination did not seize in anticipation on the good things that fate still obstinately withheld from him. On the other hand, I never noticed among the wealthier inhabitants of the United States that proud contempt for physical gratifications that is sometimes found even in the most opulent and dissolute aristocracies. Most of these wealthy men were once poor; they have felt the sting of want; they were long at the mercy of adverse fortune. Now that the victory is won, the passions that accompanied the struggle have survived it: their minds are, as it were, intoxicated by the small enjoyments they have pursued for forty years. Not that in the United States, as elsewhere, there is not a certain number of wealthy people who, having come into their property by inheritance, possess without effort an opulence they have not earned. But even these men are no less devotedly attached to the pleasures of material life. The love of well-being has now become the predominant taste of the nation. The great current of men's passions runs in that channel, and sweeps everything along with it.
